title: WhaleSpotter thermal-camera AI on a Coast Guard station at Angel Island alerts San Francisco Bay mariners and the Vessel Traffic Service to gray whales from 19 May 2026
summary: WhaleSpotter software flags gray whales in thermal camera images for a specialist to verify before alerts reach San Francisco Bay mariners, and detections had passed 16,900 by early July.
account: UC Santa Barbara announced the San Francisco Bay WhaleSpotter system on 19 May 2026. Its first thermal camera was on Angel Island. The AI flags whale heat signatures, and a marine-mammal specialist checks them. Confirmed detections appear on Whale Safe for mariners and for the Coast Guard’s Vessel Traffic Service. IEEE Spectrum attended the launch and reported on 26 May 2026 that the system had logged 6,600 detections in about a week and a half. The count includes repeated detections of the same whales. The Marine Mammal Center counted a whale found off San Leandro on 27 May 2026 among suspected or probable strike deaths. It told CBS News Bay Area that a whale found off Pier 80 on 4 June 2026 died from a suspected vessel strike. Bay Nature later visited the traffic service and described its dedicated Whale Safe screen and near-daily detections. It also described radio guidance to captains and a second camera on the ferry Lyra. That reporting establishes operational use. Inside Climate News reported on 26 July 2026 that detections had passed 16,900 by early July and that San Francisco Bay Ferry captains were receiving alerts on board. Erin Meyer-Gutbrod of the University of South Carolina told Inside Climate News that detection alone does not reduce strike risk. No source measures a reduction in strikes or links a particular alert to a documented avoided collision.
purpose: The network was built to detect whales in the bay around the clock and alert vessels so they can slow or alter course.
system: FLIR thermal cameras with WhaleSpotter AI detection, human verification and Whale Safe alert mapping
developer: WhaleSpotter (detection AI) with UC Santa Barbara's Benioff Ocean Science Laboratory
deployer: Benioff Ocean Science Laboratory with the U.S. Coast Guard Vessel Traffic Service and The Marine Mammal Center
taxonomy_note: Launch only; the aim is whale conservation, which Trustible's description reaches only as “improved environment”.

ai_role.statement: AI detects candidate whale signatures in thermal imagery. Human specialists verify them before alerts reach mariners. IEEE Spectrum adds an early detection count and the developer’s explanation of why human review remains necessary. Bay Nature independently observed the Coast Guard workflow. Neither report independently estimates the system’s effect on whale survival.

display.answer: UC Santa Barbara, home of the deploying Benioff Ocean Science Laboratory, issued the launch announcement. IEEE Spectrum, Bay Nature and Inside Climate News reported separately through interviews and visits. CBS News Bay Area reported necropsy findings from the Marine Mammal Center, one of the deployers.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: WhaleSpotter software flags gray whales in thermal camera images for a specialist to verify before alerts reach San Francisco Bay mariners, and detections had passed 16,900 by early July.
fields.account: UC Santa Barbara announced the San Francisco Bay WhaleSpotter system on 19 May 2026. Its first thermal camera was on Angel Island. The AI flags whale heat signatures, and a marine-mammal specialist checks them. Confirmed detections appear on Whale Safe for mariners and for the Coast Guard’s Vessel Traffic Service. IEEE Spectrum attended the launch and reported on 26 May 2026 that the system had logged 6,600 detections in about a week and a half. The count includes repeated detections of the same whales. The Marine Mammal Center counted a whale found off San Leandro on 27 May 2026 among suspected or probable strike deaths. It told CBS News Bay Area that a whale found off Pier 80 on 4 June 2026 died from a suspected vessel strike. Bay Nature later visited the traffic service and described its dedicated Whale Safe screen and near-daily detections. It also described radio guidance to captains and a second camera on the ferry Lyra. That reporting establishes operational use. Inside Climate News reported on 26 July 2026 that detections had passed 16,900 by early July and that San Francisco Bay Ferry captains were receiving alerts on board. Erin Meyer-Gutbrod of the University of South Carolina told Inside Climate News that detection alone does not reduce strike risk. No source measures a reduction in strikes or links a particular alert to a documented avoided collision.

value.text: The AI detects candidates automatically, but people verify sightings and decide how vessels should respond. It does not control ship steering or speed.

provenance.basis: UCSB review process and Bay Nature captain-decision discussion.
